title: JD Vance: H-1B Visas Should Go to 'Actual Geniuses,' Not Cheap Foreign Labor
excerpt: Speaking on the All-In Podcast, the Vice President defended the administration's $100,000 fee and fraud crackdown, saying H-1B visas should enrich the American economy rather than displace domestic workers — a position that closely mirrors Elon Musk's.
body:
• Vice President JD Vance told the All-In Podcast that the H-1B program should admit "actual geniuses" who enrich the U.S. economy, not let companies replace American workers with lower-paid foreign hires.
  • He defended the administration's $100,000 H-1B fee and a fraud crackdown, including new measures aimed at companies that lay off American workers while seeking H-1B staff.
  • The stance echoes Elon Musk's long-held position that the program should attract exceptional talent rather than serve as a low-cost hiring channel.
  • Indian nationals receive roughly seven in ten H-1B visas issued each year, making the overhaul the most consequential U.S. immigration change for Indian professionals in years.

WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance used a September 16 appearance on the All-In Podcast to defend the Trump administration's overhaul of the H-1B program, arguing the skilled-worker visa should go to "actual geniuses" who strengthen the American economy rather than to companies swapping domestic employees for cheaper foreign labor. The administration had acted on its own authority, he said, because "Congress is not going to pass a law changing this. There just isn't the political will to do it."

Vance said officials had reviewed fraud in the system and settled on administrative tools: the administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions and new restrictions aimed at employers that cut American jobs while applying for foreign hires. "It's a person that is going to significantly enrich the tech ecosystem or the American economy. You know, you're not just replacing one accountant who makes $60,000 with a lower-wage foreign accountant who makes $45,000 a year. That is not what the programme exists for," he said, according to ANI.

"What are the things that we can do administratively to ensure that if a tech company is going to try to get an H-1B visa, it's an actual genius."

— JD Vance, Vice President of the United States

The remarks, made during a recording at the All-In Summit, put Vance squarely in line with Elon Musk, who has long argued the program should import exceptional talent rather than undercut domestic wages, the American Bazaar reported.

A year of escalating pressure on the program

The All-In appearance is the latest step in a sustained campaign. In October 2025, Vance said H-1B visas should go to "super geniuses" whose talent America should retain, rather than being used to hire accountants "at a 50 percent discount." That December, he called it wrong for companies to bypass American workers for "cheaper options in the third world." The White House then moved unilaterally: a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, and in July 2026 the Department of Labor launched what Vance described as "dozens of subpoenas and investigations" into suspected abuse of the system, according to IndiaPost.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=eeTmJ__BLt4

President Trump has sent mixed signals throughout. Asked on Fox News whether H-1B numbers should fall to protect wages, he agreed "to some extent" but insisted America must still "bring in talent from outside" for specialized sectors — a view closer to Musk's camp than to the restrictionist wing calling for the program's elimination.

What it means for Indian professionals

India is the center of gravity for H-1B. Indians take roughly seven of every ten H-1B visas issued annually — about 60,000 of the 85,000 yearly allotment — and some 730,000 H-1B holders now live in the United States along with nearly 550,000 dependents, according to the advocacy group FWD.us. Any rewrite of the rules lands hardest on Indian engineers, analysts and researchers, and on the employers that sponsor them.

https://x.com/marketsday/status/2100198580464370089

A higher fee and fraud probes raise the bar for ordinary skilled workers even as the program remains open to elite talent. Companies with recent layoff histories face new scrutiny: Vance singled out firms that claim they "can't find the workers" after laying off "5,000 people." For Indian aspirants, the practical signal is plain — mid-skill sponsorships will be harder and costlier, while demonstrably exceptional profiles become the safest bet.

What's next

Vance acknowledged the administration has been sued over its immigration moves and expects more court fights. Roughly 20 Democratic-led states have challenged the $100,000 fee. Hospitals, universities and startups that depend on global hires for hard-to-fill roles are also pushing back, warning the fee and tighter screening will raise costs and uncertainty.

"The H-1B should not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners. It should exist to enrich the American economy. And that's exactly what we're trying to make sure it does."

— JD Vance, Vice President of the United States

With Congress out of the picture, the program's shape will be decided by administrative rules and the courts.
image_caption: U.S. Vice President JD Vance. He said H-1B visas should go to 'actual geniuses' rather than lower-paid foreign hires.
nri_angle: Indian nationals receive roughly seven in ten H-1B visas, so Vance's "genius-only" framing and the $100,000 fee reshape the single most important U.S. immigration pathway for Indian professionals and aspirants.
author: Diaspora Desk
